neighborhoods.name: Le Marais
neighborhoods.character: Medieval streets, Jewish Quarter, galleries, queer culture, and some of the best falafel on earth. Paris's most interesting neighborhood by a long margin — fashionable without being pretentious.

neighborhoods.name: Montmartre
neighborhoods.character: The village above Paris. Steep streets, artists, the vineyard, views, and Sacré-Cœur dominating the skyline. Tourist-heavy around the basilica but genuinely bohemian two streets away.

neighborhoods.name: Canal Saint-Martin
neighborhoods.character: Paris's hippest canal neighborhood. Iron footbridges, art studios, natural wine bars, record shops. Young Parisians picnic on the canal banks in summer. Nothing tourist-y.

neighborhoods.name: Saint-Germain-des-Prés
neighborhoods.character: The intellectual heart of Paris. Cafés where Sartre and de Beauvoir wrote, the Luxembourg Gardens, independent bookshops. Expensive but essential.

neighborhoods.name: Belleville
neighborhoods.character: Multicultural, working-class, the real Paris that tourists rarely find. Chinese restaurants, North African food, street art, and a view of the city from Parc de Belleville that beats the Eiffel Tower.

experiences.name: Louvre at 9am Wednesday/Friday
experiences.description: The world's largest art museum. Don't try to see it — choose a wing and go deep. The Richelieu wing (Northern European painting, French sculpture) is undervisited and extraordinary. The Mona Lisa is smaller and more crowded than you expect.
experiences.why_this_matters: The Louvre is one of the greatest achievements of human civilization. But strategy matters — most visitors see 10% and leave exhausted. See 2% with full attention.
experiences.practical_tips: Wednesday and Friday open until 9:45pm — less crowded in the evening. Book timed entry online. The Richelieu and Sully wings are better than Denon. Skip the Mona Lisa unless it matters to you.

experiences.name: Canal Saint-Martin morning walk
experiences.description: The iron footbridges and tree-lined banks of Canal Saint-Martin before the cafes open. Locals walk dogs. Bakers deliver bread by cargo bike. The canal locks occasionally operate. This is Paris without performance.
experiences.why_this_matters: Amélie was filmed here, but the canal is better than the film. Morning light on water, iron bridges, and the sound of a city waking up — this is Paris's most human hour.
experiences.practical_tips: Start at Place de la République and walk north to Stalingrad. The best stretch is between Rue du Faubourg-du-Temple and Rue de la Grange-aux-Belles. Coffee at Ten Belles.

experiences.name: Eiffel Tower at dawn (before crowds)
experiences.description: Not visiting the tower — standing beneath it at 6am when it belongs to you. Champ de Mars is empty. The tower's ironwork is extraordinary up close without a crowd. Then walk to Trocadéro for the classic view as the city wakes up.
experiences.why_this_matters: The Eiffel Tower as a tourist experience is exhausting. The Eiffel Tower at dawn, with no one else there, is genuinely magnificent. Don't pay to go up — stand below it.
experiences.practical_tips: Go at 6am or earlier in summer. The tower sparkles for 5 minutes every hour after dark (until 1am) — worth seeing once. For the classic view, walk to Trocadéro.

experiences.name: Marché d'Aligre morning market
experiences.description: Paris's most authentic food market — produce, North African spices, aged cheeses, secondhand wine, and the covered Beauvau market inside. Almost no tourists. Prices are a quarter of what you'd pay in tourist areas.
experiences.why_this_matters: This is where Parisians in this quarter actually shop. The range and quality of produce is extraordinary. Eat breakfast here from market stalls — it costs €5 and tastes like Paris.
experiences.practical_tips: Open Tue-Sun mornings until 1pm. The covered Beauvau market has excellent cheese and charcuterie. The flea market section on weekends has vintage wine and books.

experiences.name: Père Lachaise Cemetery contemplative walk
experiences.description: The most famous cemetery in the world is genuinely one of Paris's most beautiful parks. Chopin, Proust, Wilde, Morrison, Piaf — all here. In autumn, leaves cover the cobbled paths. You are never truly alone, but it still feels private.
experiences.why_this_matters: This is a profound meditation on time, art, and Paris's relationship with its own history. Oscar Wilde's tomb is covered in lipstick kisses. Jim Morrison's always has flowers.
experiences.practical_tips: Download a map — the cemetery is labyrinthine. Free entry. Go in morning for best light. Autumn is spectacular. The outer sections are less visited and more atmospheric.

experiences.name: Saint-Germain literary cafe morning
experiences.description: Café de Flore or Les Deux Magots at 8am, before the tourist photography begins. Sit outside, order a café crème and a croissant. Watch the neighborhood wake up. Sartre wrote Being and Nothingness at this table.
experiences.why_this_matters: These cafés are tourist traps by noon. At 8am they're exactly what they always were — a place where ideas and coffee intermingle. The experience is worth the price.
experiences.practical_tips: Go on a weekday. Café de Flore at 8am has a calmer atmosphere than Les Deux Magots. Order from the waiter — don't go to the bar. A coffee and croissant runs €12.

experiences.name: Musée d'Orsay impressionist galleries
experiences.description: The world's greatest Impressionist collection, housed in a spectacular converted railway station. Monet, Renoir, Degas, Van Gogh, Cézanne — all in one building. The hall itself, with its enormous clock, is one of Paris's most beautiful spaces.
experiences.why_this_matters: The Impressionists changed how humanity sees. Viewing Monet's series paintings together (haystacks, cathedral, water lilies) in sequence shows the idea they were pursuing in a way no single image conveys.
experiences.practical_tips: Thursday evenings until 9:45pm are significantly less crowded. The top floor has the best Impressionist rooms. Book online and skip the line. The café inside has a great view through the station clock.

experiences.name: Belleville street art and view
experiences.description: Belleville is where Paris hides its best street art and its most diverse food scene. Walk the Belleville murals, find the hidden garden at Parc de Belleville, and look out over Paris from a viewpoint that almost no tourist knows.
experiences.why_this_matters: The view from Parc de Belleville is better than Montmartre — higher, less crowded, free, and surrounded by actual Parisians having picnics rather than souvenir vendors.
experiences.practical_tips: Start at Belleville metro. Walk up Rue de Belleville for the murals. Parc de Belleville is at the top — go to the upper terrace for the view. Return via Rue Denoyez for concentrated street art.

experiences.name: Falafel in the Jewish Quarter (Le Marais)
experiences.description: Rue des Rosiers has the best falafel in Paris — possibly in Europe. L'As du Fallafel's falafel wrap is a Paris institution: crispy, loaded with eggplant and tahini, eaten standing on the street.
experiences.why_this_matters: Paris has extraordinary Jewish-Algerian food culture, and this is the best expression of it. At €7 for a wrap, it's also the best value meal in the 4th arrondissement.
experiences.practical_tips: L'As du Fallafel has a line — it moves fast. Get the falafel, not the shawarma. Eat standing on the street. Closed Friday afternoon and Saturday (Sabbath).

experiences.name: Luxembourg Gardens afternoon
experiences.description: The most beautiful park in Paris — formal French gardens around the Medici Fountain, students reading on green metal chairs, tennis courts, beekeeping hives, the Orangerie. On a sunny afternoon, there is no better place to be in Paris.
experiences.why_this_matters: This is what Parisians do. They sit in the metal chairs in the sun, read, talk, or simply exist. It is the Parisian art of nothing — deeply restorative.
experiences.practical_tips: Free entry. The green metal chairs are iconic — grab one by the octagonal basin. The Medici Fountain is at the east end, quieter and more intimate. Go after 2pm.

experiences.name: Montmartre pre-dawn walk to Sacré-Cœur
experiences.description: Sacré-Cœur at 5:30am, when only the devout and the insomniacs are there. The steps are empty. Paris glows below. Walk back down through Montmartre's sleeping village streets — no souvenir sellers, no sketch artists, just cats.
experiences.why_this_matters: Montmartre with tourists is one experience. Montmartre at dawn is completely different — the village it was before Paris swallowed it. The 180-degree view of Paris at dawn is the best in the city.
experiences.practical_tips: Take the funicular (free with Navigo or one metro ticket) going up so you have energy for the views. Walk down the north side through the vineyards and village streets.

experiences.name: Natural wine bar evening in the 11th
experiences.description: The 11th arrondissement invented Paris's natural wine movement. Small bistrots with handwritten menus, wine by the glass, no tablecloths. Order the 'assiette du moment' — a plate of whatever's good — and let the waiter choose the wine.
experiences.why_this_matters: This is where the culinary future of Paris is being invented. Not the tourist restaurants with Eiffel Tower views — the 40-seat bistrots where the chef is also the waiter and the menu changes daily.
experiences.practical_tips: Try Le Servan, Bistrot Paul Bert, or Septime. Book ahead — these fill fast. Don't go before 8pm. Order 'le menu' if there is one — it's always the best value.

experiences.name: Centre Pompidou and Stravinsky Fountain
experiences.description: The inside-out building that changed architecture, with the best collection of modern art in Europe. The Matisse cut-outs, the Duchamp readymades, the Surrealist rooms. Outside, the Stravinsky Fountain with Nikki de Saint Phalle's colorful sculptures is free.
experiences.why_this_matters: The Pompidou's collection (Picasso, Kandinsky, Matisse, Ernst) represents the 20th century's complete artistic revolution. The building itself remains audacious 50 years on.
experiences.practical_tips: Free entry first Sunday of every month. Top floor view is included in ticket. The escalator tubes offer views of Paris as you ride up. Closed Tuesday.

experiences.name: Île Saint-Louis evening walk and Berthillon ice cream
experiences.description: The smaller island in the Seine is quieter than Île de la Cité, lined with 17th-century hôtels particuliers, and has one ice cream shop (Berthillon) that locals consider the best in France. Walk the quays at golden hour, ice cream in hand.
experiences.why_this_matters: Paris is a city best experienced at human walking pace, at the level of water. The quays of Île Saint-Louis at dusk, with Notre-Dame behind you, is the romantic Paris of every imagination — and it's free.
experiences.practical_tips: Berthillon is often closed (they take lengthy holidays — Parisians are philosophical about this). If closed, any of the other ice cream shops on Rue Saint-Louis en l'Île have good alternatives.

experiences.name: Palais Royal gardens morning coffee
experiences.description: The Palais Royal gardens are one of Paris's most elegant secrets — a formal arcaded garden directly behind the Louvre that most tourists walking past never enter. At 9am, older Parisians read newspapers on the benches.
experiences.why_this_matters: This is the kind of place that rewards the traveler who walks through a door rather than past it. The arcades have antique shops, a theater, and small galleries. Quiet, beautiful, absolutely not on the tour buses.
experiences.practical_tips: Enter from Rue de Rivoli or Rue Saint-Honoré. Free entry to the gardens. The arcaded galleries are worth walking — one café here is better than any tourist cafe nearby.

food_scene.name: Croissant (fresh from a proper boulangerie)
food_scene.where: Any arrondissement boulangerie not near tourist sites
food_scene.tourist_trap_warning: The croissants sold in cafes near tourist attractions are inferior. Find a boulangerie with a line of locals at 8am — that's quality.

food_scene.name: Steak-frites at a classic bistro
food_scene.where: Le Relais de l'Entrecôte (no reservation, show up)
food_scene.tourist_trap_warning: Only one thing on the menu — the steak with secret sauce and unlimited frites. A queue forms outside. Worth the wait.

food_scene.name: Époisses cheese
food_scene.where: Any fromagerie in any neighborhood market
food_scene.tourist_trap_warning: The most pungent cheese in France — banned on the Paris Metro. Buy it, find a bench in a park, eat it with bread. Unforgettable.

photography_spots.name: Pont de Bir-Hakeim at sunrise
photography_spots.tip: The double-decker bridge with the Eiffel Tower behind it — used in Inception. At sunrise, no one is there.

photography_spots.name: View from Parc de Belleville
photography_spots.tip: The panoramic view of Paris from Belleville is better than Sacré-Cœur with far fewer crowds.

practical_tips.transport: Paris metro is excellent. Buy a carnet of 10 tickets or a day pass. Taxis are expensive. Walking is the best transport for the 1st through 6th arrondissements.
practical_tips.etiquette: Say 'bonjour' and 'merci' always. Parisians appreciate the effort. In restaurants, catch the server's eye — don't wave or snap fingers.
practical_tips.money: Tipping is not required but appreciated (5-10%). Most places take cards. ATMs are everywhere.
practical_tips.language: French matters here. A few words of French unlock a warmer city. 'Excusez-moi, parlez-vous anglais?' is the right way to begin.
practical_tips.best_kept_secret: The covered passages (Galerie Vivienne, Passage Jouffroy) — 19th-century glass-roofed arcades that feel like a different Paris. Almost completely tourist-free.

june.note: Excellent. Long days, outdoor terraces full.

july.note: Hot, crowded. Paris Plages on the Seine.

september.note: Best month. Fewer tourists, perfect weather.

october.note: Autumn colors, cozy cafes, beautiful light.
